name: Familial Mediterranean Fever

prevalence.estimate: 1 in 200 to 1 in 1,000 in affected populations; 1 in 100,000 in non-Mediterranean populations

criteria.description: Recurrent febrile episodes with serositis (peritonitis, pleuritis, pericarditis) lasting 1-3 days
Pathogenic MEFV gene mutations (especially M694V, M680I, V726A homozygous or compound heterozygous)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Tel-Hashomer: >= 2 major criteria, OR 1 major + 2 minor. Eurofever (2019): presence of confirmatory MEFV mutations plus compatible clinical features, OR clinical criteria in absence of genotyping.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Autosomal recessive inheritance (MEFV gene). M694V homozygosity associated with severe disease and higher amyloidosis risk. Colchicine response strongly supports diagnosis.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Recurrent episodes of fever with peritonitis lasting 1-3 days
pathognomonic.notes: Severe abdominal pain mimicking acute abdomen; self-limited in 1-3 days

common.symptomName: Monoarthritis (acute, large joint, typically knee or ankle)

common.notes: Well-demarcated erythema on shin/foot, resembles cellulitis but sterile

occasional.notes: In males; vaginalitis of tunica vaginalis

rare.notes: Most feared complication; prevented by colchicine. Presents as proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome.
Prolonged episode of severe myalgia lasting weeks

laboratory: Elevated ESR, CRP, SAA during attacks (normalize between episodes)
Proteinuria if AA amyloidosis has developed
Elevated SAA between attacks predicts amyloidosis risk
imaging: Abdominal imaging during attacks: free fluid, peritoneal thickening (often leads to unnecessary surgery)
Chest X-ray: small pleural effusion during pleuritic attacks
genetic: Common pathogenic variants: M694V, M680I, V726A, M694I, E148Q
Autosomal recessive (some heterozygotes may be symptomatic)
M694V homozygosity: most severe phenotype, highest amyloidosis risk
other: Colchicine therapeutic trial: dramatic reduction in attack frequency strongly supports diagnosis
Genetic testing: identifies ~70-80% of cases (some have unidentified mutations)
Rectal or abdominal fat biopsy if amyloidosis suspected

distinguishingFeatures: TRAPS has longer attack duration (1-4 weeks vs 1-3 days in FMF)
TRAPS may have periorbital edema and migratory rash
AOSD has quotidian fever, salmon rash, markedly elevated ferritin
AOSD is not episodic with full resolution between episodes
Appendicitis is a single acute episode, not recurrent
Appendicitis has progressive course without spontaneous resolution

redFlags: Proteinuria in FMF patient (screen for AA amyloidosis)
Attacks mimicking acute abdomen leading to unnecessary surgery
Failure to respond to colchicine (consider alternative diagnosis or non-compliance)
Chronic arthritis (suggests more severe phenotype, consider biologic therapy)
references: Livneh A, et al. Criteria for the diagnosis of familial Mediterranean fever. Arthritis Rheum. 1997;40(10):1879-1885.
Gattorno M, et al. Classification criteria for autoinflammatory recurrent fevers. Ann Rheum Dis. 2019;78(8):1025-1032.
Ozen S, et al. EULAR recommendations for the management of familial Mediterranean fever. Ann Rheum Dis. 2016;75(4):644-651.
